1.0.0.en: A servant of God: a humble expression from Paul, which also means that his life and ministry belong to God. The elect of God: those whom God, by His foreknowledge, knows will believe. This encourages Bishop Titus that among his people there are those who will believe, so he is encouraged in preaching to them; and on the other hand, he is not to be proud if they believe, ascribing the credit to himself, because it is God who chose them.

1.0.1.en: After godliness: not a theoretical knowledge about God, as the Gnostics who followed them proclaim, but a knowledge applied in the life of the bishop and the people.

1.0.2.en: In humility Paul declares the goal of his life, which is the service of God; he is an apostle, consecrated to preaching the Christian faith and the practical spiritual life filled with righteousness and goodness.

1.1.0.en: In hope: in the original Greek, “resting in hope.”

1.1.1.en: Who cannot lie: God is true in His promises, and is not like the gods of Crete, which were known for lying, and which consequently made the people of Crete characterized by lying.

1.1.2.en: God promised those who believe in Him a blessed eternity with Him, and this was in the heart of God before the foundation of the world: to create man and let him enjoy the Kingdom with Him, and His promises are true. This hope makes the believers labor to acquire virtue and bear sufferings for the sake of holding fast to the faith to the end.

1.2.0.en: The Lord Jesus came with salvation at a time appointed by God the Father, who saw in His infinite wisdom that it was the most suitable of times. He chose the Apostle Paul to be entrusted with preaching this salvation which the Lord accomplished.

1.3.0.en: My own son: this shows how close Titus was to Paul's heart, and in the Coptic translation it is “my beloved son.”

1.3.1.en: The Apostle addresses his epistle to Titus, his true believing son, in the one common faith that was delivered once to the saints, which is the faith of the whole Church, and which unites Jews and Gentiles who have come to know the right faith.

1.3.2.en: St. Paul the Apostle concludes the opening of the epistle with the apostolic blessing, which includes the gifts of grace for the believer and his enjoyment of mercy and inner peace, whose source is God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior.

1.3.3.en: Consider what your goal in life is, so that you do not lose sight of it. If your goal is the salvation of your soul, then give sufficient time to your relationship with God and hasten to repent so that you remain in your purity; and if it is also the service of God, then seize every opportunity to offer your love to everyone you meet.

1.4.s.en: (2) The qualities of the bishop and the priest

1.4.0.en: I left you in Crete: this means that Paul preached in Crete together with his disciple Titus, but in order to complete the preaching he left Crete, and Titus remained in it to complete the ministry there. Therefore Titus is considered the bishop of Crete, or its archbishop, responsible for its pastoral care.

1.4.1.en: That you should set in order the things that are wanting: there was not enough time to organize the Church in Crete fully, and Paul taught Titus orally what concerns these arrangements. This shows the importance of apostolic tradition, that is, the oral teachings from the Apostles to their successors down to this day, in addition to the teachings of the Holy Bible. And ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed you: one of the most important arrangements is the appointment of shepherds. Paul had charged Titus with this, and here he confirms their appointment, that is, their ordination and consecration for the ministry. The correct translation of the word “elders” is “priests,” and it means all the priestly ranks, including bishops, priests and deacons.

1.4.2.en: It is noted that Crete had many cities at that time, about a hundred cities, as Homer the poet says.

1.4.3.en: St. Paul the Apostle reminds Titus of his pastoral responsibility as a bishop over Crete, to teach the people and to arrange the ministry there, especially the ordination of priests.

1.5.0.en: St. Paul mentions in the verses (6 to 9) the conditions for the bishop or the priest, which are:

1.5.1.en: 1- Blameless: he means the visible sins that cause stumbling, and not any sin whatever, for there is not a single man who is perfectly righteous.

1.5.2.en: 2- The husband of one wife: if his wife has died, he does not marry a second time after becoming a widower; but at the Council of Nicaea (in the year 325 AD) the Fathers decided that the bishop must be a celibate.

1.5.3.en: What is meant by not marrying a second time is chastity: if he married the first marriage because of the need of nature, let him be content with this if his wife dies, and let him live for God and for the upbringing of his children, if he has any. A second and third marriage is not forbidden to the members of the people, but whoever comes forward to the priestly ranks must be more chaste than his people.

1.5.4.en: 3- Having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly: whoever has cared for the upbringing of his physical children is fit to shepherd the children of the Church. So the children of the one who comes forward to the priestly rank must be bound to the faith and to obedience to the Church, and must not have evil desires that cause people to complain about them.

1.6.0.en: For a bishop must be: this confirms that the word “elders” in (v. 5) means the bishops and the priests, and not the priests only.

1.6.1.en: Blameless, as the steward of God: he is responsible before God for shepherding the people and will give an account of his stewardship before God. He is the image of God, so he must be without a sin that causes the people to stumble.

1.6.2.en: 4- Not self-willed: not selfish or conceited, so he cares for his people before himself and does not domineer over them, but is humble and bears with everyone, just as Christ was humble and called us to follow His example (Mt 11:29).

1.6.3.en: 5- Not soon angry: the bishop meets many provoking problems, but he must control himself; and even if he is firm, or inner anger assails him, he must not cause those around him to stumble and fall into excessive anger.

1.6.4.en: 6- Not given to wine: not accustomed to drinking wine, for he may need wine as a medicine, as it was used anciently because there were not enough medicines. What is meant is not being absorbed in material pleasures.

1.6.5.en: 7- No striker: that is, one who strikes much. Even if in some cases and special situations he resorts to severity, he must not be hasty or frequent in striking. What is meant is not harshness, but gentleness and feeling for the people and encouraging them.

1.6.6.en: 8- Not greedy of filthy lucre: he is not to be a lover of money or accept gain by illegitimate ways, but on the contrary to be chaste and ascetic, content with the least possible of material needs and not a lover of possessions and ownership.

1.7.0.en: In this verse he moves to the positive conditions for the bishop, and says:

1.7.1.en: 9- A lover of hospitality: a lover of everyone, who cares for those who have no one to care for them.

1.7.2.en: 10- A lover of good men: like Christ his Lord, who went about everywhere doing good; so he looks for works of mercy, and if he finds a problem he is not annoyed by it but tries to solve it.

1.7.3.en: 11- Sober: that is, balanced, not impulsive in his words or actions, but understanding and examining everything calmly.

1.7.4.en: 12- Just: inclined to a pure life, purifying himself always by repentance and adorning himself with virtues.

1.7.5.en: 13- Holy: keeping away from evils, and fearing God and revering Him.

1.7.6.en: 14- Temperate: he uses everything in due measure and does not indulge any evil desire, and is careful in his thought, his sight, his speech and his deeds.

1.8.0.en: 15- Able to exhort: he learns in order to be able to teach continually according to the sound doctrine he received from the Fathers, and to rebuke the heretics and not leave them to corrupt the thought of his people with their perverted opinions.

1.8.1.en: Examine yourself in light of these conditions with which you ought to be adorned, whether you are a servant or one of the members of the people, and be sure that these virtues are an interlinked chain, each leading to the others. So begin with the virtue you find yourself most in need of, and it will lead you to the rest.

1.9.0.en: Unruly: members of the Church who do not submit to the teachings of the priests and servants.

1.9.1.en: Vain: false teachings foreign to the teachings of the Church.

1.9.2.en: They of the circumcision: Christians of Jewish origin.

1.9.3.en: To clarify the words of St. Paul in (v. 9) about one of the conditions of the bishop or the priest, which is that he be able to exhort with sound doctrine and to convict the gainsayers, he alerts his disciple Titus to the existence of Christians of Jewish origin who, after accepting faith in Christ, still proclaim the necessity of holding to Jewish teachings such as circumcision and abstaining from certain foods, all of which were types of the New Testament. The evil of these people appears in:

1.9.4.en: 1- Their insistence on false teachings and their not submitting to the leadership of the Church.

1.9.5.en: 2- Their promoting their false ideas, so they deceive some of the simple members of the Church.

1.10.0.en: Whose mouths must be stopped: answering them and persuading them with arguments and proofs, so that they find no word with which to answer in their error.

1.10.1.en: Who subvert whole houses: they lead entire families astray, parents and children, and draw them away from the upright faith.

1.10.2.en: Teaching things which they ought not: teachings that deviate from the right faith.

1.10.3.en: Filthy lucre: exploiting those who follow them to collect money from them.

1.10.4.en: St. Paul the Apostle decides that these innovators must be stopped from repeating their stumbling talk, because by their teachings they lead entire Christian families astray; and moreover they are greedy, seeking to gain the money which they collect from their followers whom they lead astray.

1.11.0.en: One of themselves: the poet Epimenides, one of the seven famous sages of Greece, who lived in the sixth century BC.

1.11.1.en: A prophet of their own: they considered these famous poets and sages to be in the rank of prophets. Evil beasts: they were distinguished by violence and fierceness.

1.11.2.en: Slow bellies: gluttonous in their love of foods, and sensual.

1.11.3.en: St. Paul wanted to alert his disciple Titus to be wary of the evils of the Cretans, so he used the words of one of their famous poets, whose words they honor and believe, who describes them as accustomed to lying and inclined to violence and bodily desires, especially the love of foods.

1.12.0.en: Paul declares his agreement with this poet's judgment of the Cretans. His purpose in these words is to alert Titus, the shepherd of this island, to rebuke the believers so that they are not carried away into the sins to which they were formerly accustomed, which can draw them away from the upright faith so that they perish.

1.13.0.en: He charges his disciple Titus to warn the believers not to listen to the teachings of the innovators, who are the Christians of Jewish origin, who proclaim the necessity of holding to circumcision and the customs of the Law in order to obtain salvation. For these innovators, after they believed, turn away from faith in Christ the Savior, claiming that the Jewish types are a condition for salvation.

1.14.0.en: The Apostle declares the thought of Christianity, which proclaims that all foods are clean because God is their Creator; so whoever believes this is pure of heart, and these foods become clean and pure to him. As for the Mosaic Law, when it forbade certain foods, that was because they signify uncleanness, but they are not unclean in themselves. The types came to an end with the beginning of the New Testament.

1.14.1.en: But the innovators and those who follow them, and every man who walks in evil, have had their hearts defiled and use foods to satisfy their own desires, so they become unclean to him because his heart has been defiled by thoughts of evil. And of course if there is any evil, it is unclean and we should not walk in it, especially if the commandment forbids it, such as adultery and theft...

1.14.2.en: And partaking of foods with purity and a pure heart does not conflict with fasting, because whoever fasts in Christianity is certain that everything is clean, but he gives it up out of devotion to the love of God and prayer, then returns to using it at times other than fasting, confirming its cleanness.

1.14.3.en: May you purify your thought from every evil, look for the virtues of others and deal with them as the image of God, so that you are pure in your glances, your words and all your actions. Even if they wrong you, keep the calm of your heart and your purity toward them, and your prayers for them will restore them to their purity and keep the devil's wars away from them, and will also protect you from his attacks, because of your purity, your humility and your holding fast to God.

1.15.0.en: The false teachers claim to have great knowledge of God, more than the rest of the believers in the Church, but sadly this knowledge is theoretical and some of their beliefs are perverted. Indeed they are far from God, as shown by their evil works, which God does not command; so in His sight they are wicked and unclean, and toward the Church they are unruly and disobedient to its teachings, and they are unfit for any good work because their hearts have been filled with evil.

1.15.1.en: Be careful to carry out the commandments of God which you proclaim or teach to others, so that your speech is from open experience and is beneficial to you and to those who hear you.

1.15.2.en: Counsels for the different groups of the people

2.0.0.en: The Apostle Paul charges his disciple Titus to proclaim the upright teachings of the faith, so as to enlighten minds and expose the error of the perverted teachings of the innovators.

2.0.1.en: Take care to teach those around you, especially your children, everything that is right, for if you fall short in this they will learn wrong things from society and from the wicked. So fortify them with sound teaching in all areas of life and do not despise their youth.

2.1.0.en: St. Paul gave special commandments for the older men, for their bishop Titus to teach them, and they are:

2.1.1.en: 1- Sober: so they do not make light of sins, relying on their steadiness because of their old age, for man is liable to fall at any time; so he must guard against the sources of sin into which the young can fall.

2.1.2.en: 2- Grave: having a steadiness and dignity that befits their age in all their speech and conduct, so they do not slip into the sins of folly and levity.

2.1.3.en: 3- Temperate: they walk with a steadiness and wisdom that befits their age.

2.1.4.en: 4- Sound in faith: they do not rush after the teachings of the innovators but hold fast to the upright teachings of the Church, since they are a reference point and an example for the young.

2.1.5.en: 5- In charity: the elderly are distinguished by fatherly tenderness, so it is easy for them to offer love to those younger than themselves, and they need to guard against the selfishness that fights them because of their fear and anxiety for themselves.

2.1.6.en: 6- In patience: the elderly suffer from a weakness of longsuffering and little flexibility, and so they fall easily into anger; so he charges them to be patient with the behavior of others that they do not like and are not accustomed to, and even to make excuses for them, because the circumstances of the young today may be different from what they themselves met when they were at that age.

2.2.0.en: Likewise the Apostle Paul teaches his disciple Titus to charge the older women to be:

2.2.1.en: 1- In behavior as becometh holiness: the old woman must not neglect herself because of her old age and become occupied with many garments and adornment, or be lax in her words and levity, and so be far from the holy conduct that befits the daughters of God.

2.2.2.en: 2- Not false accusers: because of their few tasks due to old age, they may spend a long time resting and so condemn others much in their conversation.

2.2.3.en: 3- Not given to much wine: it seems that wine drinking was widespread in Crete, accompanied by abundance of foods; so he warns the old women not to make light of it and go too far in drinking wine, which leads to their drunkenness, and this does not befit them as believers and is against the commandments of God.

2.2.4.en: 4- Teachers of good things: on the positive side, it befits them, because of their old age, to do good works and to encourage others to do good; indeed let this be their primary work instead of wasting time on what is not fitting.

2.2.5.en: May you look at everything you have learned from God in your past life, to thank Him and to live by these teachings, and also to teach them to others, so that your life is filled with doing good.

2.3.0.en: Titus is responsible for charging the old women, after they are adorned with holiness and steadiness, so that they can teach the young women, because as women they understand the young women among them; and so that the bishop is not exposed to speaking with the young wives about private problems which they are shy to speak about with him; and so that no one looks wrongly at the bishop as if he had some purpose in speaking with these young women. So he asks the old women to teach the young wives the following:

2.3.1.en: 1- To love their husbands: so they show their love for their husbands by kind words and deeds that give a good atmosphere in the home, understanding between the spouses, and an inclination to giving and self-sacrifice.

2.3.2.en: 2- To love their children: in caring for their needs and showing motherhood and sufficient care. This satisfies not only the children but the mothers themselves, because whoever gives love to others is satisfied first.

2.4.0.en: 3- Discreet: they walk with steadiness and wisdom.

2.4.1.en: 4- Chaste: they control their desires in clothing, food, the love of acquiring things, and everything.

2.4.2.en: 5- Keepers at home: they are occupied with the needs of their homes. This brings them out of selfishness to care for the comfort of those with them in the home, and they provide an atmosphere of love that gives the family rest, and it protects them from falling into the strange thoughts of the world that arise from emotional emptiness.

2.4.3.en: 6- Good: they incline to doing good and to every work useful to others.

2.4.4.en: 7- Obedient to their own husbands: the first demand of any man is respect and appreciation, so a woman's submission to her husband gives him rest and makes him ready to sacrifice his opinions out of love for his wife, who is humble in her submission. In this way the family lives bound together, and unbelievers cannot find any complaint or faults in the families of the believers, so as to describe Christians as failures in married life and thereby be a curse upon the name of Christ.

2.5.0.en: As for the young men, he teaches them not to be impulsive in their conduct and speech because of their youth, and to guard against desires and temptations, so that they are disciplined and steady in everything.

2.6.0.en: St. Paul charges his disciple Titus to be an example to the young men, indeed to the whole Church, in:

2.6.1.en: A - Good works: works of goodness and disciplined, steady conduct.

2.6.2.en: B - Doctrine: his Christian teaching is characterized by the following:

2.6.3.en: 1- Uncorruptness: that is, he has no personal purpose but only to make known the name of Christ and the salvation of souls.

2.6.4.en: 2- Gravity: steady words that befit respect for the word of God and the steadiness of the teacher.

2.6.5.en: 3- Sincerity: so he cares for the good of those who hear and devotes himself to serving them.

2.6.6.en: 4- Sound speech, that cannot be condemned: that is, upright teaching free from error and the ideas of the world, so unbelievers cannot find any fault in it with which to condemn it.

2.6.7.en: You are the light of the world and the salt of the earth, and without realizing it you are an example to those around you. So be careful in your words and conduct so that you cause no one to stumble, but draw them to Christ even without speaking.

2.7.0.en: He also charges the slaves to walk well so as to be an example to their masters, and even to be able to draw them to the faith, or at least to the glorification of their God, as Potiphar perceived concerning Joseph his servant. So he asks of the slaves:

2.7.1.en: 1- Submission to the orders of their masters and not to object to them in anything, except of course what is contrary to the commandments of God.

2.7.2.en: 2- Honesty and not stealing, whether from the possessions of the houses in which they serve or from the business affairs in which their masters employed them, so they trade or practice any craft for the benefit of their masters.

2.7.3.en: For it was easy for them to steal from these without the masters knowing, but he demanded of them complete honesty, so that they show thereby the loftiness of Christianity, adorn it with their virtues and glorify Christ in their lives.

2.7.4.en: Do not make light of your position, however small you are in age, standing or abilities, for your faithfulness in your life with God affects those around you. Indeed Christ humbly declares His need of your virtues, so that He may be glorified in you and His teachings be adorned by your good conduct.

2.8.0.en: In order that the Apostle may support the different groups of the people and give them strength to carry out the preceding counsels, he declares that the grace of God which appeared in Christ the Redeemer on the Cross is offered to all mankind, so that everyone who believes in Christ and lives in the Church enjoys the support of this grace in all his speech and conduct.

2.9.0.en: This divine grace supports us in two directions:

2.9.1.en: 1- Negative: it is the rejection of evil desires and ungodliness, that is, treating sin as permissible and boasting of it.

2.9.2.en: 2- Positive: it is walking with steadiness and discipline, that is, with prudence and an inclination to good works, and also godliness, that is, the fear of God and walking in holiness in the days of our life on earth in preparation for eternal life.

2.10.0.en: Looking for that blessed hope: waiting for the Second Coming of Christ encourages the souls that suffer, so they bear it with patience, and it drives the believers with zeal in all the spiritual practices and makes them despise the desires of the world.

2.10.1.en: The glorious appearing of the great God: on the day of the Lord's coming His glory will appear in a way that surpasses all imagination, to all people in the whole world, delighting His children and frightening the wicked. This glory may be in the form of a great light and praising angels and things we cannot grasp now.

2.10.2.en: Our Savior Jesus Christ: in the midst of this great glory our Lord Jesus Christ Himself appears to embrace His children and lift them up to glory.

2.10.3.en: Hope in the Second Coming of Christ with His light and glory encourages all who suffer for His sake.

2.11.0.en: Who gave Himself for us: the Christ who appears in His great glory is our beloved God who died for us on the Cross to buy us with His blood with a love that cannot be expressed.

2.11.1.en: That He might redeem us from all iniquity: the purpose of offering His life for us is to save us from all our sins and bear them for us on His Cross.

2.11.2.en: And purify unto Himself a peculiar people: those who believe in Him become pure, living in righteousness, clinging to Him as members of His body, which is the Church, and distinguished from the world by following Him and being united with Him. Zealous of good works: because of the divine love poured out for the believers, they are moved with zeal to do what pleases God, which is good works.

2.11.3.en: The great Christ in His Second Coming is Himself our loving Christ who gave Himself for us to cleanse us from our sins and sanctify us for His love and for doing good.

2.12.0.en: These things speak and exhort: Paul directs his disciple to teach his people the preceding teachings in this chapter, and to explain and exhort with these words on every spiritual occasion.

2.12.1.en: And rebuke with all authority: whoever contradicts these teachings, be firm with him and rebuke him that he may repent, and speak with the authority of the bishop given to you by Christ to shepherd His people.

2.12.2.en: Let no man despise you: do nothing unseemly that would make them despise you, and speak with confidence in Christ who speaks through your tongue, however much the opponents resist you.

2.12.3.en: He charges him to teach all the preceding teachings and to rebuke whoever rejects them, trusting in the power of God which is with him despite his youth.

2.12.4.en: Look every day to Christ who is coming to take you to glory, so that you leave every sin behind and are zealous to do good with every person. Let this be a daily training for you, so that it changes your life and increases your longing for the Kingdom. Closing counsels
